abraham: First of the three patriarchs and the father of the Jewish people.
abraham-accords: Normalization agreements signed in 2020 between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, followed by Morocco and Sudan.
abu-ghosh: Arab village west of Jerusalem, known for its Crusader-era church and for its good relations with Jewish neighbors in 1948.
acre: Ancient port on the northern coast, also called Akko.
aelia-capitolina: Name of the Roman city that Hadrian founded on the ruins of Jerusalem about 130 CE.
arab-citizens-of-israel: Muslim, Christian and Druze Arabs who hold Israeli citizenship, about a fifth of the population.
armistice-agreements-1949: Four separate ceasefire agreements signed in 1949 between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria, ending the Independence, War of.
ashkenazim: Jews descended from the communities of Central and Eastern Europe, and by extension of Western Europe and the Americas.
beta-israel: The Jewish community of Ethiopia, brought to Israel mainly in Operation Moses in 1984 and 1985 and Operation Solomon in 1991.
census: A full count of residents. Israel held its first in 1948. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics counted the West Bank and Gaza in 1997, 2007 and 2017.
central-bureau-of-statistics: Israel’s official statistics office, set up in 1949.
druze: An Arabic-speaking community with its own religion, living mainly in the Galilee, on Carmel, Mount and on the Golan Heights.
fertility-rate: The average number of children a woman is expected to have in her lifetime.
green-line: The 1949 armistice line between Israel and its neighbors, named for the green pencil used on the map.
haredim: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who follow a strict interpretation of Jewish law and often live in separate communities.
histadrut: The General Federation of Labor, founded in 1920.
jewish-agency: The body recognized under the British Mandate to represent the Jewish community.
kibbutz: A collective settlement where property is held in common.
knesset: Israel’s parliament of 120 members, elected by proportional vote.
masorti: Traditional. In Israeli surveys the term describes Jews who keep some religious observance without being strictly Orthodox, a group between secular and religious.
mass-immigration: The wave of 1948 to 1951, when about 700,000 immigrants arrived and roughly doubled the Jewish population.
mizrahim: Jews descended from communities of the Middle East and North Africa.
moshav: A cooperative farming village in which each family works its own plot and markets produce together.
natural-increase: The growth of a population from births over deaths, apart from migration.
palestinian-central-bureau-of-statistics: The statistics office of the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah.
sabra: A Jew born in Israel, named for the prickly pear, tough outside and sweet inside.
sephardim: Jews descended from the communities of Spain and Portugal, expelled in the 1490s.
settlements: Israeli communities built since 1967 in the West Bank.
west-bank: The territory west of the Jordan River held by Jordan from 1948 and captured by Israel in 1967.
yaacov-agam: Artist born in Rishon LeZion in 1928 and a pioneer of kinetic art.
s-y-agnon: Hebrew novelist, 1888 to 1970, born in Galicia, who lived in Jerusalem for most of his life.
ahab: King of Israel from about 874 to 853 BCE, son of Omri and husband of Jezebel.
ahad-haam: Pen name of the essayist Asher Ginsberg, 1856 to 1927, who argued that the land should become a spiritual and cultural center for the Jewish people.
ahavat-zion: Novel by Abraham Mapu published in 1853, set in Jerusalem in the time of Isaiah.
ain-jalut: Spring in the Jezreel Valley where the Mamluks defeated the Mongols in 1260 and stopped their advance toward Egypt.
aleppo-codex: Manuscript of the Hebrew Bible with vowel signs, written in Tiberias about 920 and long held in Aleppo.
alexander-jannaeus: Hasmonean king from 103 to 76 BCE who enlarged the kingdom to near the size of David's.
alexander-the-great: Macedonian king who conquered the Persian Empire.
aliyah: Immigration of Jews to the land of Israel, from the Hebrew word for "ascent." Historians count successive waves from 1882…
first-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1882 to 1903, mostly from Eastern Europe.
second-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1904 to 1914, mostly from Russia.
third-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1919 to 1923, about 35,000 people, mostly young pioneers from Eastern Europe after the First World War.
fourth-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1924 to 1929, about 80,000 people, mostly middle-class families from Poland.
fifth-aliyah: Wave of Jewish immigration from 1929 to 1939, mostly from Germany and Central Europe, as Nazi persecution grew.
yehuda-alkalai: Sephardic rabbi, 1798 to 1878, who urged Jews to return to the land as a practical first step toward redemption.
alliance-isra-lite-universelle: Paris-based Jewish organization founded in 1860 that ran schools across the Middle East.
natan-alterman: Poet, 1910 to 1970, born in Warsaw, who came to the land in 1925.
amarna-letters: Clay tablets of about 1350 BCE from Egypt, letters from Canaanite rulers including the king of Jerusalem asking the pharaoh for help.
yehuda-amichai: Poet, 1924 to 2000, born in Würzburg, who lived in Jerusalem.
amos: Prophet of the 8th century BCE, a shepherd from Tekoa near Bethlehem, who denounced injustice in the northern kingdom.
antiochus-iii: Seleucid king from 222 to 187 BCE who took Judea from the Ptolemies in 198 BCE and let the Jews live by their ancestral laws.
antiochus-iv: Seleucid king from 175 to 164 BCE who banned Jewish practice and defiled the Temple.
apollonia-arsuf: Coastal site north of Herzliya with Crusader fortifications and traces of earlier Persian and Roman towns.
arab-league: Organization of Arab states founded in Cairo in 1945, now with 22 members.
arab-revolt: Arab uprising against British rule and Jewish immigration from 1936 to 1939.
arad: Negev town founded in 1962 beside the ruins of ancient Arad, a Canaanite city and later a fortress of Judah.
yasser-arafat: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization from 1969 and first head of the Palestinian Authority.
mordecai-ardon: Painter, 1896 to 1992, born in Galicia, who studied at the Bauhaus under Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky.
ariel: City in the hills of Samaria founded in 1978, home to Ariel University.
aristobulus-i: Hasmonean ruler who in about 104 BCE was the first to take the title of king.
ashdod: Port city south of Tel Aviv, and today Israel's largest port.
ashkelon: Coastal city that was a major Philistine port and later a Crusader fortress.
assyria: Empire in northern Mesopotamia that dominated the region in the 9th to 7th centuries BCE.
war-of-attrition: Low-level war of 1967 to 1970 between Israel and Egypt along the Suez Canal.
robert-aumann: Mathematician born in Frankfurt in 1930 and a professor at the Hebrew University.
autoemancipation: Pamphlet of 1882 by Leo Pinsker that argued Jews must seek independence themselves and not wait for others to grant it.
avdat: Nabataean city in the Negev on the Incense Route, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
babylon: Ancient city on the Euphrates in today's Iraq.
return-from-babylon: Return of Jewish exiles to Judea after Cyrus the Greatconquered Babylon in 539 BCE.
balfour-declaration: Letter of 2 November 1917 in which the British government expressed support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
banias: Springs at the foot of Mount Hermon that feed the Jordan.
bar-kokhba-revolt: Jewish revolt against Rome from 132 to 135 CE.
daniel-barenboim: Pianist and conductor born in Buenos Aires in 1942 and raised in Israel.
netta-barzilai: Israeli singer who won the 2018 Eurovision Song Contest with the song "Toy."
basel: Swiss city where Theodor Herzl held the First Zionist Congress in 1897.
bauhaus: German school of architecture and design, 1919 to 1933.
mount-of-beatitudes: Hill above the Sea of Galilee where Christian tradition places the Sermon on the Mount.
beer-sheva: Largest city of the Negev, where Abrahammade a covenant with Abimelech, according to Genesis 21.
menachem-begin: Israeli prime minister from 1977 to 1983 and former head of the Irgun.
beit-el: Biblical site where Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching heaven.
beit-shean: City at the junction of the Jordan and Jezreel valleys.
david-ben-gurion: Leader of the Jewish community before independence, who declared the state on 14 May 1948 and was Israel's first prime minister.
ben-sira: Jerusalem sage who wrote the Wisdom of Ben Sira, also called Sirach, about 180 BCE.
eliezer-ben-yehuda: Lexicographer, 1858 to 1922, who settled in Jerusalem in 1881 and led the revival of Hebrew as a spoken language.
naftali-bennett: Israeli prime minister from 2021 to 2022, heading a coalition of eight parties.
beth-shearim: Town in the lower Galilee with a great Jewish burial ground.
bethlehem: Bethlehem is the town south of Jerusalem where David was born and where Christian tradition places the birth of Jesus.
bezalel-school: Art school founded in Jerusalem in 1906, the first Jewish art academy in the land.
hayim-nahman-bialik: Hebrew national poet, 1873 to 1934, who settled in Tel Aviv in 1924.
biltmore-conference: Zionist conference in New York in 1942 that demanded a Jewish commonwealth in the land and an end to the White Paper of 1939.
british-mandate: British rule over the land, assigned by the League of Nations and lasting from the 1920s until May 1948.
bronze-age-collapse: Wave of destruction about 1200 BCE that ended Egyptian rule in Canaan and toppled many cities of the eastern Mediterranean.
burma-road: Makeshift supply road built in the spring of 1948 to bypass the Latrun roadblock and break the siege of Jerusalem.
bus-18-bombings: Two suicide bombings of the No.
byzantines: The eastern Roman Empire, which ruled the land from the 4th century.
caesarea: Port city built by Herod between about 22 and 10 BCE and later the Roman capital of Judea.
camp-david-accords: Framework agreements signed in 1978 by Menachem Begin and Egypt's Anwar Sadat that led to the 1979 peace treaty and Israel's return of the Sinai.
cana: Village in the lower Galilee where, according to the New Testament, Jesusturned water into wine at a wedding.
canaan-land: Biblical name of the land west of the Jordan before the Israelite settlement, home of the Canaanites.
canaanites: Peoples of the land before the Israelites, organized in city- states such as Hazor and Megiddo, and known for the early alphabet.
capernaum: Fishing village on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught.
carmel-market: Tel Aviv's main open-air market, called the Shuk HaCarmel, in use since the 1920s.
mount-carmel: Coastal ridge above Haifa. The Bible places the contest of Elijah with the prophets of Baal there.
operation-cast-lead: Israeli campaign in Gaza from December 2008 to January 2009 after years of rocket fire.
castel-national-park: Hilltop west of Jerusalem where Israeli forces fought in April 1948 to open the road to the city.
marc-chagall: Painter, 1887 to 1985, born in Belarus and based in France.
city-of-david: Oldest part of Jerusalem, on the ridge south of the Temple Mount above the Gihon Spring.
coastal-plain: Fertile strip along the Mediterranean from Gaza to Mount Carmel.
coastal-road-massacre: Attack of 11 March 1978 in which Fatah gunmen landed from the sea, hijacked a bus on the coastal highway and killed 38 civilians, 13 of them children.
constantine: Roman emperor from 306 to 337 who legalized Christianity in 313.
crusaders: European Christian armies who took Jerusalem in 1099 and held parts of the land until the Mamluks took Acre in 1291.
crusades: Series of European Christian military campaigns to take Jerusalem, beginning in 1095.
damascus-affair: Blood libel of 1840 in Damascus in which Jews were falsely accused of murder.
dana-international: Israeli singer born in 1972 who won the 1998 Eurovision Song Contest with the song Diva.
david: Second king of Israel, about 1000 BCE.
tower-of-david: Citadel by the Jaffa Gate with remains from the Hasmonean to the Ottoman periods.
moshe-dayan: Israeli general and politician, 1915 to 1981, who lost an eye fighting in Lebanon in 1941.
dead-sea: Salt lake between Israel and Jordan, about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land on earth.
dead-sea-scrolls: About 900 manuscripts found in caves near Qumran, written from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE.
deborah: Prophet and judge of Israel who led the tribes to victory over the Canaanites, as told in the Book of Judges and in the Song of Deborah.
song-of-deborah: Victory poem in Judges 5 celebrating Deborah and the defeat of a Canaanite army.
operation-defensive-shield: Israeli operation in Judea and Samaria in spring 2002, launched during the Second Intifada after a wave of suicide bombings.
degania: First kibbutz, founded in 1909 on the southern shore of the Sea of Galilee by immigrants of the Second Aliyah.
dolphinarium-bombing: Suicide bombing of 1 June 2001 outside a beachfront discotheque in Tel Aviv that killed 21 people…
dome-of-the-rock: Shrine with a golden dome on the Temple Mount, completed in 691 CE by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik.
dreyfus-affair: French scandal of the 1890s in which a Jewish army officer was falsely convicted of treason.
mount-ebal: Mountain north of Shechem, paired with Mount Gerizim.
egypt: Neighbor to the southwest. It ruled Canaan in the Bronze Age, fought Israel in 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973…
adolf-eichmann: Nazi official who organized the deportation of Jews to the death camps.
eilat: Israel's southernmost city, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea.
ein-gedi: Oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea with springs and waterfalls.
ein-kerem: Village in the hills southwest of Jerusalem, traditionally the birthplace of John the Baptist.
ein-zivan: Kibbutz in the southern Golan Heightsfounded after 1967 and known for its vineyards.
arik-einstein: Israeli singer, 1939 to 2013, whose songs from the 1960s onward made him a leading voice of Israeli pop and rock.
eli: High priest at Shiloh and mentor of the prophet Samuel, according to 1 Samuel.
elijah: Prophet of the 9th century BCE who opposed Ahab and Jezebel.
elisha: Prophet of the 9th century BCE and successor of Elijah, who served in the northern kingdom.
entebbe: Town in Uganda whose airport was the scene of the Entebbe raidin 1976.
entebbe-raid: Israeli commando operation of 4 July 1976 that freed hostages held by hijackers at Entebbe Airport in Uganda.
levi-eshkol: Israeli prime minister from 1963 until his death in 1969.
eurovision-song-contest: Annual European song contest. Netta Barzilai won it for Israel in 2018, and Israel has won four times.
ezra: Scribe who, according to tradition, led a group of exiles back from Babylon about 458 BCE and taught the Torah in Jerusalem.
fatimids: Dynasty of Egyptian caliphs who conquered the land in 969.
galilee: Region of northern Israel with hills, valleys and the Sea of Galilee.
sea-of-galilee: Freshwater lake about 21 kilometers long, about 210 meters below sea level, and Israel's main reservoir.
gamla: Fortress town in the Golan Heights that fell to the Romans after a siege in 67 CE.
gaza: Ancient coastal city and Philistine center on the Mediterranean, today the Gaza Strip.
battle-of-gaza: Battle of 1917 in which British forces took Gaza from the Ottomans and opened the way to Jerusalem.
gaza-border-kibbutzim: Farming communities within a few kilometers of the Gaza Strip, among them Be'eri, Kfar Aza and Nir Oz.
disengagement-from-gaza: Israel's withdrawal in 2005 from Gaza and from four settlements in northern Samaria.
mount-gerizim: Mountain above Shechem, holy to the Samaritans and the place of the blessings in Deuteronomy.
garden-of-gethsemane: Olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives where, according to the New Testament, Jesus prayed the night before his arrest.
gezer: Ancient city on the road between Jerusalem and the coast.
golan-heights: Basalt plateau between the Galilee and Syria.
leah-goldberg: Poet and children's author, 1911 to 1970, born in Königsberg, who settled in Tel Aviv in 1935.
goliath: Philistine warrior from Gath whom the young David killed with a sling, as told in 1 Samuel 17.
first-revolt: Jewish rebellion against Rome from 66 to 73 CE.
nahum-gutman: Painter, sculptor and author, 1898 to 1980, who came to the land with his family in 1905 and grew up in the new city of Tel Aviv.
habima-theatre: Hebrew-language theater founded in Moscow in 1917 and settled in Tel Aviv in 1931.
haganah: Underground Jewish defense force of the British Mandate, founded in the early 1920s.
haggai: Prophet of about 520 BCE who urged the returned exiles to rebuild the Second Temple.
haifa: Israel's third largest city, on the slopes of Mount Carmel.
hamas: Palestinian Islamist movement founded in 1987 that has ruled Gaza since 2007.
hanukkah: Eight-day festival of lights that marks the rededication of the Temple in 164 BCE after the Maccabean Revolt.
hasidism: Pietist movement that began in Eastern Europe in the 18th century.
hatikvah: Israel's national anthem. Its words come from the poem Tikvatenu by Naftali Herz Imber of 1878, and its melody is a folk tune.
ofra-haza: Israeli singer, 1957 to 2000, born to a Yemenite Jewish family in Tel Aviv.
hazor: Canaanite city in the Upper Galilee.
hebrew-bible: The Jewish scriptures in three parts, the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings.
hebrew-university: Israel's first university, begun on Mount Scopus in 1918 and opened in 1925.
hebron: City in the Judean hills with the Cave of the Patriarchs, the traditional burial place of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob…
hellenization: Spread of Greek language and culture after Alexander the Great.
mount-hermon: Highest mountain in the region, 2,814 meters, on the border of Syria and Lebanon.
herod-the-great: Roman client king of Judea from 37 to 4 BCE.
herodium: Fortress and palace that Herod built on an artificial hill south of Jerusalem.
avram-hershko: Biochemist born in Hungary in 1937 who came to Israel as a boy.
theodor-herzl: Viennese journalist, 1860 to 1904, founder of political Zionism.
herzliya: Coastal city north of Tel Aviv, founded in 1924 and named for Theodor Herzl.
moses-hess: German Jewish socialist, 1812 to 1875, whose book Rome and Jerusalem of 1862 called for a Jewish state.
hezbollah: Lebanese Shia militia and political party formed in 1982 with Iranian support.
hezekiah: King of Judah around 715 to 686 BCE.
hittites: Anatolian empire that clashed with Egypt at Battle of Kadeshabout 1274 BCE.
holocaust: Nazi Germany's murder of six million Jews in Europe from 1941 to 1945.
church-of-the-holy-sepulchre: Church in the Old City built over the traditional sites of the crucifixion and burial of Jesus.
hosea: Prophet of the 8th century BCE in the northern kingdom, shortly before the fall of Samaria.
lovers-of-zion: Jewish groups formed in Russia and Romania from the 1880s to promote settlement in the land.
bronislaw-huberman: Polish violinist, 1882 to 1947, who founded the Palestine Symphony Orchestra in 1936.
hula-valley: Valley of the upper Jordan in the Galilee, drained in the 1950s and partly restored as a nature reserve.
hurva-synagogue: Synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, destroyed in 1948 and rebuilt in 2010.
hyksos: Foreign rulers of northern Egypt from about 1650 to 1550 BCE, many of them Canaanite in origin.
israel-defense-forces: Israel's army, navy and air force, formed in May 1948 from the Haganah and other forces.
naftali-herz-imber: Poet, 1856 to 1909, whose poem Tikvatenu of 1878 became the words of Hatikvah.
war-of-independence: War from 1947 to 1949 that followed the UN Partition Plan and Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948.
first-intifada: Palestinian uprising against Israeli rule that began in December 1987 and lasted until about 1993.
second-intifada: Palestinian uprising that began in September 2000 and brought a wave of suicide bombings.
iran: Country east of Iraq, heir of the Persian Empire.
iraq: Modern state in ancient Mesopotamia, home of Babylon and Assyria.
irgun: Underground Jewish organization of the Mandate years, led from 1944 by Menachem Begin.
iron-dome: Israeli air-defense system in use since 2011 that intercepts short-range rockets and shells.
isaac: Son of Abraham and second of the three patriarchs.
isaiah: Prophet who lived in Jerusalem in the 8th century BCE, a counselor of Hezekiah.
israel: The Jewish state, declared on 14 May 1948, with Jerusalem as its capital.
israel-museum: Jerusalem museum opened in 1965 with collections of archaeology, art and Judaica.
jacob: Third patriarch, renamed Israel, whose twelve sons became the tribes.
palestine-symphony-orchestra: Orchestra founded in 1936 by the violinist Bronislaw Huberman to employ Jewish musicians who had fled Europe.
merneptah-stele: Victory monument of the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah, about 1208 BCE.
israelites: The descendants of Jacob, the people of the twelve tribes and of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
jaffa: Ancient port south of Tel Aviv, among the oldest in the world.
jaffa-port: Harbor of ancient Jaffa, where cedar logs for Solomon's Temple arrived, according to 2 Chronicles.
marcel-janco: Romanian-born artist, 1895 to 1984, and a founder of the Dada movement in Zurich.
jehu: King of Israel from about 841 to 814 BCE.
jeremiah: Prophet in Jerusalem before and after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BCE who warned of the city's fall.
jericho: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the lowest on earth, in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea.
jerusalem: Capital of Israel and the holiest city of Judaism.
east-jerusalem: Part of Jerusalem east of the 1949 armistice line, including the Old City.
jerusalem-of-gold: Song written by Naomi Shemer and first sung in May 1967.
old-city-of-jerusalem: Walled area of about one square kilometer, with the Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian quarters.
siege-of-jerusalem-701-bce: Assyrian siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE under Sennacherib.
jerusalem-talmud: Commentary on the Mishnah completed in the Galilee about 400 CE.
jesus: Jewish teacher from the Galilee who was crucified in Jerusalem about 30 CE under Pontius Pilate.
jewish-brigade: Unit of the British Army formed in 1944 from volunteers from the Jewish community of the Mandate.
jewish-national-fund: Organization founded in 1901 to buy land for Jewish settlement.
the-jewish-war: Account of the revolt against Rome by Josephus, written about 75 CE.
jezebel: Phoenician princess who married Ahab and became queen of Israel.
jordan: Kingdom east of the Jordan River.
jordan-river: River of about 250 kilometers that runs from springs near Mount Hermon through the Hula Valley and the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea.
josephus: Jewish general in the Galilee who surrendered to Rome and wrote The Jewish War about 75 CE.
joshua: Successor of Moses who led the Israelites across the Jordan, according to the Bible.
josiah: King of Judah from about 640 to 609 BCE who centralized worship in Jerusalem and reformed the faith.
rabbi-judah-the-prince: Leader of the Jewish community in the Galilee about 200 CE who compiled the Mishnah.
judah-maccabee: Leader of the Maccabean Revolt after 166 BCE.
judea: Southern hill country around Jerusalem, named for the tribe of Judah and the kingdom of Judah.
judea-and-samaria: Central hill country between the Jordan Valley and the coastal plain, the heartland of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
judean-hills: Hill country west and south of Jerusalem, with villages, kibbutzim and sites from the battles of 1948.
kadesh: Ancient city on the Orontes River in Syria.
battle-of-kadesh: Clash about 1274 BCE between Ramses II and the Hittites on the Orontes River in Syria.
daniel-kahneman: Psychologist, 1934 to 2024, born in Tel Aviv and trained at the Hebrew University.
joseph-karo: Scholar, 1488 to 1575, who settled in Safed and wrote the Shulchan Aruch, the most widely accepted code of Jewish law.
katzrin: Town in the Golan Heights founded in 1977.
etgar-keret: Writer of short stories and film scripts, born in Ramat Gan in 1967.
kiryat-anavim-and-maale-hahamisha: Two of the first kibbutzim in the Judean Hills, founded in 1920 and 1938.
ephraim-kishon: Satirist and film director, 1924 to 2005, born in Budapest.
western-wall: Retaining wall of the Temple Mount platform from the time of Herod.
lachish: Fortified city of Judah southwest of Jerusalem.
lachish-reliefs: Stone reliefs from the palace of Sennacherib at Nineveh showing the siege and fall of Lachish in 701 BCE.
latrun: Hill and monastery on the road to Jerusalem.
lebanon: Neighbor to the north. Israel fought wars in Lebanon in 1982 and 2006, and Hezbollah is based there.
lebanon-war-1982: Israeli invasion of Lebanon in June 1982 to push out the PLO.
second-lebanon-war: War of July and August 2006 between Israel and Hezbollah after the group abducted two Israeli soldiers.
lod-airport-massacre: Attack of 30 May 1972 at Lod Airport, now Ben-Gurion Airport…
lots-cave: Cave near the southern shore of the Dead Sea where, according to tradition, Lot and his daughters took refuge after the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah.
maalot-massacre: Attack of 15 May 1974 in which three gunmen of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized a school in the northern town of Ma'alot.
maccabean-revolt: Jewish uprising that began in 167 BCE against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV and his ban on Jewish practice.
maccabees: Family of the priest Mattathias and his sons who led the Maccabean Revolt.
madaba-map: Mosaic floor map of the 6th century in a church at Madaba, Jordan, made between 542 and 570.
madrid-peace-conference: Conference of October 1991 that for the first time brought Israel and its Arab neighbors into direct talks.
magdala: Fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, home of Mary Magdalene.
mahane-yehuda-market: Jerusalem's main open-air market, known as the Shuk, founded in the 1880s.
makhtesh-ramon: Largest of the Negev's erosion craters, about 40 kilometers long and up to 9 kilometers wide.
mamluks: Slave-soldier dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria.
abraham-mapu: Lithuanian Hebrew writer, 1808 to 1867, whose novel Ahavat Zion (1853) set a love story in the time of Isaiah and is counted the first modern Hebrew novel.
masada: Mountain fortress above the Dead Sea built by Herod.
mea-shearim: Neighborhood of Jerusalem founded in 1874 and now home to ultra-Orthodox Jews who keep the customs of Eastern Europe.
megiddo: Ancient mound that guarded a pass between the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley.
pharaoh-merneptah: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1213 to 1203 BCE, son of Ramses II.
mesopotamia: Land between the Tigris and Euphrates, the cradle of Babylonand Assyria.
mikveh-israel: Agricultural school founded near Jaffa in 1870 by the Alliance Israelite Universelle.
mishkenot-shaananim: Row of houses built in 1860 with funds from Moses Montefiore, the first Jewish neighborhood outside the walls of the Old City.
mishnah: Code of Jewish oral law, compiled about 200 CE in the Galilee by Rabbi Judah the Prince.
mongols: Central Asian armies that invaded Syria in 1260.
moses-montefiore: British philanthropist, 1784 to 1885, who visited the land seven times and funded Mishkenot Sha’ananim…
moses: Leader who took the Israelites out of Egypt and received the Torah at Sinai, according to the Bible.
munich-olympics-massacre: Murder of eleven Israeli athletes and coaches by Palestinian gunmen at the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich.
shechem: Ancient city near modern Nablus, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
nachmanides: Rabbi Moses ben Nahman, 1194 to 1270, a Spanish scholar who reached Jerusalem in 1267 and re-established its Jewish community.
nahlaot: Cluster of old neighborhoods near Mahane Yehuda Market, with narrow lanes, stone houses and small synagogues.
joseph-nasi: Portuguese-born Jewish courtier, 1510 to 1579, who served the Ottoman sultan.
nation-state-law: Basic Law passed in 2018 that defines Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people.
league-of-nations: International organization created after the First World War.
nazareth: Largest Arab city in Israel, in the lower Galilee.
negev: Desert in the south that covers more than half of Israel's land.
nehemiah: Jewish official of the Persian court who came to Jerusalem about 445 BCE and rebuilt its walls, according to the Book of Nehemiah.
netanya: Coastal city founded in 1929 and known for its beaches and diamond industry.
benjamin-netanyahu: Israeli prime minister, first elected in 1996 and the longest serving in the country's history.
neve-tzedek: First Jewish neighborhood outside Jaffa, founded in 1887 and now a quarter of galleries and boutiques within Tel Aviv.
the-north: Region of the northern coast and the Galilee, from Rosh Hanikra to Mount Carmel and the Golan Heights.
october-7-2023-attack: Attack by Hamas on southern Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and about 250 taken hostage.
ofakim: Negev town founded in 1955, settled by immigrants from North Africa.
old-jaffa: Historic quarter of Jaffa with stone alleys, galleries and the Church of St.
mount-of-olives: Ridge east of the Old City with the oldest continuously used Jewish cemetery and the Garden of Gethsemane at its foot.
omri: King of Israel from about 880 BCE who founded Samaria as his capital.
osirak-reactor: Iraqi nuclear reactor near Baghdad that Israeli aircraft destroyed in June 1981.
oslo-accords: Agreements of 1993 and 1995 between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization that set up the Palestinian Authority.
ottomans: Turkish dynasty that ruled the land from 1517 to 1917.
ovadiah-of-bertinoro: Italian rabbi, about 1445 to 1515, who reached Jerusalem in 1488 and revived its community.
palestine-exploration-fund: British society founded in 1865 to survey the land.
palestine-liberation-organization: Umbrella organization of Palestinian groups founded in 1964 and led by Yasser Arafat from 1969.
palestinian-authority: Self-government body set up under the Oslo Accords in 1994 that administers parts of Judea and Samaria.
abel-pann: Painter, 1883 to 1963, born in Latvia as Abba Pfeffermann.
park-hotel-massacre: Suicide bombing of 27 March 2002 at a Passover seder in the Park Hotel in Netanya that killed 30 civilians.
un-partition-plan: United Nations resolution of 29 November 1947 proposing a Jewish and an Arab state with Jerusalem under international rule.
paul: Jewish apostle from Tarsus who carried the Christian message across the Roman world and visited Jerusalem several times.
peel-commission: British commission of 1937 that first proposed splitting the land into a Jewish and an Arab state.
shimon-peres: Israeli statesman, 1923 to 2016, who served as prime minister, foreign minister and ninth president.
itzhak-perlman: Violinist born in Tel Aviv in 1945, who had polio as a child.
persia: Ancient empire centered in today's Iran.
perushim: Disciples of the Vilna Gaon who settled in Jerusalem and Safedfrom 1808 and formed an early community of Ashkenazi Jews there.
petah-tikva: Town east of Tel Aviv founded in 1878, called the "mother of the colonies" because it was the first modern Jewish agricultural village.
philistines: Seafaring people who settled the southern coast about 1175 BCE.
phoenician-alphabet: Alphabet of 22 consonant letters from the Phoenician coast, taking shape about 1050 BCE.
pontius-pilate: Roman prefect of Judea from about 26 to 36 CE, who ordered the crucifixion of Jesus.
leo-pinsker: Odessa physician, 1821 to 1891, whose pamphlet Autoemancipation of 1882 urged Jews to seek a homeland of their own.
pompey: Roman general who took Jerusalem in 63 BCE and began Roman rule in the land.
operation-protective-edge: Seven-week Israeli campaign in Gaza in July and August 2014, in response to rocket fire and tunnel attacks.
psalms: Collection of 150 hymns in the Hebrew Bible, traditionally credited to David.
ptolemies: Greek dynasty of Egypt that ruled the land from 301 to 198 BCE until Antiochus III took it.
qarqar: Ancient city in Syria where the Battle of Qarqar was fought in 853 BCE.
battle-of-qarqar: Battle of 853 BCE in Syria where a coalition including Ahab of Israel halted the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III.
qumran: Settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea.
quneitra-viewpoint: Lookout over the abandoned Syrian town of Quneitra on the Golan Heights.
rabin-kings-of-israel-square: Central square of Tel Aviv, renamed after Yitzhak Rabin who was assassinated there on 4 November 1995.
yitzhak-rabin: Israeli general and prime minister who signed the Oslo Accords.
ramses-ii: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1279 to 1213 BCE who fought the Hittites at Battle of Kadesh.
ramses-iii: Egyptian pharaoh from about 1186 to 1155 BCE who defeated the Sea Peoples at the edge of the Nile Delta.
rehovot: City south of Tel Aviv, home of the Weizmann Institute of Science founded by Chaim Weizmann.
reim: Kibbutz near the Gaza border. Hundreds were killed at the Nova music festival nearby on 7 October 2023.
law-of-return: Law of 1950 that gives every Jew the right to immigrate to Israel and become a citizen.
rishon-lezion: Town south of Tel Aviv founded in 1882 by immigrants of the First Aliyah.
david-roberts: Scottish painter, 1796 to 1864, who toured the land in 1839 and 1840.
romans: The rulers of the land from 63 BCE, who put down the Jewish revolts and destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE.
rosh-hanikra: Chalk cliffs and sea grottos on the Lebanese border at the northern end of Israel's coast.
rothschild-boulevard: Tree-lined avenue in Tel Aviv from the city's first years.
edmond-de-rothschild: French banker, 1845 to 1934, who funded early farming villages in the land, including Rishon LeZion.
reuven-rubin: Painter, 1893 to 1974, born in Romania, who settled in the land in 1923.
safed: Hill city in the Upper Galilee.
saladin: Muslim sultan who defeated the Crusaders at the Horns of Hattin and retook Jerusalem in 1187.
salome-alexandra: Hasmonean queen who ruled from 76 to 67 BCE, widow of Alexander Jannaeus.
samaria: Northern hill country of the heartland, with the capital of the kingdom of Israel at Sebastia and the old city of Shechem.
fall-of-samaria: Capture of the capital of the northern kingdom by Assyria in 722 BCE.
san-remo-conference: Meeting of the Allied powers in Italy in April 1920 that assigned the Mandate for the land to Britain.
sarah: Wife of Abraham and the first of the matriarchs, buried with him in the Cave of the Patriarchs at Hebron.
sarona-market-and-hostage-square: Food market in a restored German Templer colony in Tel Aviv.
sataf: Hillside near Jerusalem with ancient terraces and springs, now a nature reserve.
saul: First king of Israel, about 1050 BCE, anointed by the prophet Samuel.
sbarro-bombing: Suicide bombing of 9 August 2001 at the Sbarro pizzeria on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem that killed 15 people, seven of them children.
mount-scopus: Ridge north of the Old City with the Hebrew University and Hadassah hospital.
scud-attacks: Iraqi missile attacks on Israeli cities during the 1991 Gulf War.
sde-boker: Kibbutz in the Negev where David Ben- Gurion lived after leaving office and where he is buried.
sderot: Town near the Gaza Strip, founded in 1951.
sea-peoples: Seafaring raiders who disturbed the eastern Mediterranean about 1200 BCE.
sebastia: Village in Samaria on the site of the capital of the kingdom of Israel, founded by Omri.
seleucids: Greek dynasty of Syria that took the land from the Ptolemies in 198 BCE and ruled until the Maccabean Revolt gained independence.
seljuk-turks: Turkic dynasty that took Syria and the land in the 1070s from the Fatimids.
septuagint: Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made in Alexandria from the 3rd century BCE for Jews who no longer read Hebrew.
gilad-shalit: Israeli soldier captured by Hamas in 2006 and held in Gaza for five years.
yitzhak-shamir: Israeli prime minister in 1983 and 1984 and again from 1986 to 1992.
ariel-sharon: Israeli general and prime minister from 2001 to 2006.
dan-shechtman: Materials scientist born in Tel Aviv in 1941 who works at the Technion.
naomi-shemer: Israeli songwriter, 1930 to 2004, who wrote Jerusalem of Goldshortly before the Six-Day War.
shfela: Rolling foothills between the coastal plain and the Judean hills, with fortress cities such as Lachish.
shiloh: Hill town where the Tabernacle stood for centuries before the Temple.
pharaoh-shishak: Egyptian pharaoh Shoshenq I, who raided Judah and Israel about 925 BCE and took tribute from Jerusalem, according to 1 Kings 14.
shrine-of-the-book: The white-domed building of the Israel Museum that holds the Dead Sea Scrollsand the Aleppo Codex.
shulchan-aruch: Code of Jewish law written by Joseph Karo in Safed and published in 1565.
sinai: Desert peninsula between Egypt and Israel, where the Bible places the giving of the Torah.
six-day-war: War of June 1967 in which Israel took the Sinai, Gaza, the Golan Heights, Judea and Samaria and East Jerusalem.
sodom-and-gomorrah: Cities of the plain that, according to Genesis 19, were destroyed by fire.
solomon: Son and successor of David, king of Israel about 970 to 930 BCE.
first-temple: The Temple built by Solomon in Jerusalem, traditionally about 960 BCE, and the center of Israelite worship.
straits-of-tiran: Narrow channel at the southern tip of the Sinai that controls access to Eilat.
suez-crisis: War of 1956 in which Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal.
suleiman-the-magnificent: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566 who rebuilt the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem in the 1530s.
sykes-picot-agreement: Secret 1916 agreement between Britain and France to divide the Ottoman Middle East into spheres of influence.
syria: Neighbor to the northeast. It fought Israel in 1948, 1967 and 1973, and Israel took the Golan Heights from it in 1967.
syria-palaestina: Roman name for the province that Hadrian created after the Bar Kokhba revolt, replacing Judaea.
valley-of-tears: Valley on the Golan Heights where Israeli tanks stopped a Syrian armored assault in the Yom Kippur War.
technion: Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, founded in 1912 and opened in 1924.
tel-aviv: City founded in 1909 on sand dunes north of Jaffa.
tel-aviv-jaffa: The united municipality of Tel Aviv and Jaffa, formed in 1950.
tel-aviv-promenade: Seaside walkway about 14 kilometers long linking Jaffa to northern Tel Aviv.
tel-dan-stele: Fragment of a victory inscription found at Tel Dan in 1993 and dated to the 9th century BCE.
first-destruction-of-temple: The burning of Solomon's Temple and of Jerusalem by Babylonin 586 BCE, followed by the exile of much of the population.
second-temple: Rebuilt and completed in 515 BCE after the return from Babylon.
temple-mount: Platform in the Old City of Jerusalem where the First Temple and Second Templestood.
tiberias: City on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, founded about 20 CE.
anna-ticho: Artist, 1894 to 1980, born in Brno, who came to Jerusalem in 1912.
timna-park: Desert park north of Eilat with copper mines worked for several thousand years…
titus: Roman general whose army destroyed Jerusalem in 70 CE, later emperor.
torah: The five books of Moses, the first part of the Hebrew Bible.
arturo-toscanini: Italian conductor who led the first concert of the Palestine Symphony Orchestra in 1936.
mark-twain: American writer who toured the land in 1867.
tzuba: Kibbutz in the Judean Hills near Crusader ruins, founded in 1948.
caliph-umar: Second caliph of Islam, who took Jerusalem in 638 and, according to tradition, let Jews settle there again.
umayyads: First Islamic dynasty, ruling from Damascus from 661 to 750.
vespasian: Roman general who began crushing the Jewish revolt in 67 CE and became emperor in 69.
vilna-gaon: Rabbi Elijah of Vilna, 1720 to 1797, the leading Torah scholar of Eastern Europe.
wadi-qelt: Canyon between Jerusalem and Jericho with a Greek Orthodox monastery, St.
chaim-weizmann: Chemist and Zionist leader, 1874 to 1952, who helped win the Balfour Declaration and became the first president of Israel in 1949.
welcome-to-zion: Companion book by Richard J. Koret, an illustrated tour of the sites of Israel…
western-wall-tunnels: Passages beneath the Muslim Quarter that follow the Western Wall for about 500 meters, exposing Herodian stonework.
white-city-of-tel-aviv: Some 4,000 buildings in the Bauhaus and International styles built in the 1930s and 1940s, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2003.
white-paper-of-1939: British policy statement that limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years and then required Arab consent.
kaiser-wilhelm-ii: German emperor who visited Jerusalem in 1898.
yad-vashem: Israel's Holocaust memorial and research center in Jerusalem, established by law in 1953.
yavne: City on the coastal plain. After 70 CE, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai founded an academy there that preserved Jewish learning after the fall of the Second…
a-b-yehoshua: Novelist, 1936 to 2022, born in Jerusalem, whose books include Mr.
yehuda-halevi: Spanish poet and philosopher, about 1075 to 1141…
yom-kippur-war: War of October 1973 in which Egypt and Syria attacked Israel on the holiest day of the Jewish year.
ada-yonath: Israeli crystallographer who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for mapping the structure of the ribosome.
zechariah: Prophet of about 520 BCE who, with Haggai, urged the rebuilding of the Second Temple.
zion: Biblical name of Jerusalem, and by extension of the whole land of Israel.
mount-zion: Hill just outside the walls of the Old City, associated with the Last Supper and with the tomb of King David.
zionism: Movement for the Jewish return to the land of Israel and national renewal there.
first-zionist-congress: Meeting called by Theodor Herzl in Basel in August 1897 that founded the organized Zionist movement and set its goal as a home for the Jewish people in…
philistia: The coastal plain of southern Canaan held by the Philistines from about 1175 BCE, centered on the five cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath.
moab: Kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon and Zered rivers in present-day Jordan, with its capital at Dibon.
edom: Kingdom in the highlands south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan and the Negev, linked in the Bible with Esau.
ammon: Kingdom east of the Jordan River with its capital at Rabbath Ammon, today's Amman, the capital of Jordan.
aram-damascus: Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus, the main rival of the northern kingdom of Israel from the ninth to the eighth century BCE.
phoenicia: Coastal city-states of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos on today's Lebanese coast…
nabataeans: Arab trading people whose kingdom, centered on Petra in present-day Jordan…
samaritans: Small community that keeps its own version of the Torah and holds Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, to be the place chosen for worship.
essenes: Jewish sect of the Second Temple period that, according to Josephus and other ancient writers, lived in strict communities…
pharisees: Jewish movement of the Second Temple period that stressed study and the oral law alongside the written Torah.
sadducees: Priestly and aristocratic party of the Second Temple period that accepted only the written Torah and rejected the oral law.
zealots: Name given to Jewish rebel factions in the revolt against Rome of 66 to 73 CE, known as the First Revolt.
sanhedrin: Council of Jewish sages and judges that served as the highest court and legislature of Jewish life.
diaspora: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel.
abbasids: Dynasty of caliphs that overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad.
twelve-tribes-of-israel: The tribes descended from the sons of Jacob according to the Bible, each with its own territory in the land.
yishuv: Hebrew word for settlement, used for the organized Jewish community in the land before the state of 1948.
decapolis: League of ten Greek-speaking cities of the Roman era, mostly east of the Jordan River in present-day Jordan and Syria.
declaration-of-independence: The proclamation of the State of Israel, read by David Ben-Gurion on 14 May 1948 in the Tel Aviv Museum on Rothschild Boulevard…
siege-of-jerusalem-1948: From early 1948 Arab forces cut the only road from the coast to Jerusalem at Bab al-Wad, leaving about 100,000 Jews short of food, water and ammunition.
altalena-affair: In June 1948, during the first truce of the War of Independence…
jewish-communities-lost-in-1948: During the War of Independence a number of Jewish communities fell or had to be abandoned.
divided-jerusalem: From 1948 to 1967 Jerusalem was split between Israel and Jordan.
waiting-period-1967: The three tense weeks before the Six-Day War.
battle-for-jerusalem-1967: On 5 June 1967 Jordan opened fire on West Jerusalem despite Israeli messages urging it to stay out of the war.
temple-mount-status-quo: The arrangement set by Moshe Dayan days after the Six-Day War.
western-wall-plaza: The open square in front of the Western Wall.
un-resolution-242: UN Security Council resolution of 22 November 1967, after the Six-Day War.
hebron-after-1967: Jews lived in Hebron for centuries until the 1929 massacre, in which 67 were killed, and the last families left in 1936.
gush-katif: The bloc of Jewish communities in the southern Gaza Strip, founded from the 1970s along the coast.
sabra-and-shatila-massacre: From 16 to 18 September 1982, during the Lebanon War (1982)…
pollard-affair: Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy intelligence analyst, was arrested in November 1985 for passing classified documents to Israel.
israel-egypt-peace-treaty: Signed on 26 March 1979 at the White House by Menachem Begin and Anwar Sadat, with President Jimmy Carter as witness, following the Camp David Accords.
taba: Beach resort at the head of the Gulf of Eilat, just south of the city.
narrow-waist: Between 1949 and 1967 Israel's coastal plain near Netanya was only about 15 kilometers wide, from the armistice line to the sea.
aliyah-bet: Clandestine immigration to the Land of Israel from 1934 to 1948, in defiance of British limits, above all the White Paper (1939).
operation-magic-carpet: The 1949 to 1950 airlift that brought about 49,000 Jews from Yemen and Aden to Israel.
operation-ezra-and-nehemiah: The 1951 to 1952 airlift of about 120,000 Jews from Iraq, after Iraq let them leave on condition that they give up their citizenship.
operation-moses: The secret airlift of about 8,000 Ethiopian Jews, known as Beta Israel, from refugee camps in Sudan to Israel between November 1984 and January 1985.
operation-joshua: A US-led airlift in March 1985, also called Operation Sheba…
operation-solomon: On 24 and 25 May 1991, as rebel forces closed in on Addis Ababa, Israel flew 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to Israel in about 36 hours.
aliyah-from-the-soviet-union: In the 1970s, after a long struggle by Soviet Jews and their supporters abroad, about 160,000 were allowed to move to Israel.
aliyah-from-north-africa: From 1948 through the 1960s most of the Jews of Morocco, Tunisia and Libya moved to Israel, while most Algerian Jews went to France.
iranian-jews: One of the oldest Jewish communities, dating back to the Persia of Cyrus the Great.
aliyah-from-france: French Jews, the largest Jewish community in Europe, began moving to Israel in larger numbers after 2000 as antisemitic attacks rose…
aliyah-from-ukraine: Immigration from Ukraine rose after the war in the east of the country began in 2014 and surged after Russia's invasion in February 2022.
aliyah-from-latin-america: Jews from Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico and other countries have moved to Israel since 1948…
bnei-menashe: A community in the northeast Indian states of Manipur and Mizoram that holds it descends from the tribe of Manasseh, one of the Twelve Tribes of Israel.
nefesh-bnefesh: Nonprofit founded in 2002 by Rabbi Yehoshua Fass and Tony Gelbart to help Jews from North America and Britain move to Israel.
jewish-agency-for-israel: Founded in 1929 to represent the Jewish people to the British Mandate authorities and build the national home.
taglit-birthright-israel: Program founded in 1999 by the philanthropists Charles Bronfman and Michael Steinhardt with the Israeli government and Jewish communities abroad.
israel-national-trail: A hiking trail of about 1,100 kilometers that crosses the whole country, from Kibbutz Dan near the Lebanese border to Eilat on the Red Sea.
jesus-trail: A walking route of about 65 kilometers opened in 2008 that links places from the life of Jesus in the Galilee.
way-of-the-patriarchs: The ancient road along the ridge of the central hill country, from Be'er Sheva through Hebron…
gideon: Judge of Israel from the tribe of Manasseh, whose story is told in Judges 6 to 8.
mount-sodom: A ridge about 11 kilometers long on the southwest shore of the Dead Sea, made largely of rock salt and still below sea level at its top.
dimona: Town in the Negev founded in 1955 and settled mainly by immigrants from North Africa.
shivta: Ruins of a town of the Nabataeans and Byzantines in the western Negev, with three churches, streets and houses still standing.
negev-bedouin: About 300,000 Bedouin Arab citizens of Israel who live in the Negev.
